source_text: Ecce enim breviter respondeo adeo nos Christi medicinam parvulis, quos innocentes novimus, non negare, ut illos potissimum copiosiore ea indigere fateamur. Nascuntur enim exigui, debiles, qui non solum ali proprio labore non possint, verum nec implorare queant opem parentum, qui tam multis casibus obnoxii sunt, ut eis etiam lac densius et lactantium plerumque somnus exitio sit.
pass_a_gloss: For behold I briefly answer that so far we do not deny the medicine of Christ to little ones, whom we know innocent, that we confess those especially to need it more copiously. For they are born tiny, weak, who not only cannot be fed by their own labor, but cannot even implore the help of parents, who are liable to so many chances that even thicker milk and often the sleep of those nursing is destruction to them.

lemmas.lexica: LS parvulus; Blaise infants without usus rationis
LS medicina; Blaise of Christ as physician

pass_b_english: Here is my brief answer: far from denying Christ’s medicine to infants, whom we know to be innocent, we acknowledge that they especially need it in greater abundance. They are born tiny and weak, unable not only to feed themselves through their own labor but even to ask their parents for help. They are exposed to so many accidents that even milk that is too thick, and often the sleep of those nursing them, can cause their death.

choices.why: Speechless newborns without rational choice; Julian's test case against inherited sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied.
